source.title: A Little Help Goes a Long Way: Efficient LLM Training by Leveraging Small LMs
source.authors: A. S. Rawat; Veeranjaneyulu Sadhanala; A. Rostamizadeh; Ayan Chakrabarti; Wittawat Jitkrittum; Vladimir Feinberg; Seungyeon Kim; Hrayr Harutyunyan; Nikunj Saunshi; Zachary Nado; Rakesh Shivanna; Sashank J. Reddi; A. Menon; Rohan Anil; Sanjiv Kumar

page_placements.theme: A weaker teacher used alongside ground-truth labels (reverse or weak-teacher distillation, weak feedback to an already supervised model)

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether a weaker language model can help a larger one through soft-label distillation, but in pre-training rather than the original fine-tuning setting and without computing PGR.
record.gate_note: The paper reports pre-training comparisons using a weaker SLM as teacher and evaluates the resulting LLMs against the SLM and standard-pretraining baseline. It also reports comparisons of SALT design choices. SFT results use downstream task labels rather than weak labels, so they are not recorded as weak-to-strong results.
record.test_reason: The 2.8B student always gets ground-truth next-token supervision: weight 1−ω=0.333 during KD, then pure ground truth. Its edge over the 1.5B teacher is therefore not weak-to-strong generalization; the gold-trained Baseline also beats the teacher. No condition trains a strong model on weak labels alone, and no PGR is computed. The question studied is a different construct: whether weak-teacher KD as an auxiliary signal beats standard gold-label pre-training. Burns et al. is cited only in related work.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that KD from a smaller LM early in pre-training, then standard training (SALT), improves 2.8B LLM quality. It reaches Baseline with under 70% of steps (about 28% wall-clock saving) and gives consistent SFT gains. SLM-based data selection helps further. Full-duration KD (RKD) underperforms Baseline. A bias-variance risk bound motivates the selective KD. A better-trained SLM teacher further improves results.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses token-level soft-label KD from a smaller LM during LLM pre-training, usually mixed with ground-truth next-token loss, and then switches to standard pre-training. It is not fine-tuning on weak labels alone and does not calculate PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: Results depend on the KD-to-standard-training transition point: average few-shot performance is reported as stable for nKD from 20K to 60K and substantially worse at 208K. Outcomes also vary across evaluation domains and between SALT and SALTDS.

fits_no_version.finding: Early-phase KD from a 1.5B SLM, mixed with gold labels and then switched to pure gold-label training, beats standard gold-label pre-training of a 2.8B LM (average 47.94/48.26 vs 47.32). Full-duration KD (RKD) falls below Baseline (44.39).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A weaker teacher's soft labels, used briefly alongside ground truth, can improve a stronger model's pre-training over gold-only training; prolonged use hurts.

fits_no_version.finding: A bias-variance bound: KD from a weaker teacher reduces loss variance at the cost of bias from teacher-truth divergence, motivating KD only on easy regions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Theory of when weak-teacher KD helps a student trained with ground truth.

fits_no_version.finding: A better-trained SLM teacher (498K steps) raises SALT's average to 48.70 from 47.94 (Appendix Table 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Teacher quality affects gains from weak-teacher KD in pre-training.

record.problems: The paper does not compute PGR or directly test fine-tuning on weak labels alone. It reports no uncertainty estimates for the tabulated comparisons. The student size is fixed in the main experiments, and there is no shift, chess, reward-modelling, or vision test.
record.rows_left_out: The limit of 60 rows was not exceeded. Left out the per-benchmark entries from Appendix Table 5, additional transition-strategy scores in Appendix Table 8, bucketed easy/medium/hard results in Table 4 and Appendix Tables 9–11, improved-teacher results in Appendix Table 6, and SFT outcomes in Table 3. The first sets are more granular or additional settings than the domain aggregates recorded here; Table 3 uses downstream fine-tuning labels rather than weak-label supervision.

untested.parts: No strong model trained on weak labels alone; no strong ceiling or PGR.
No method compared against naive weak-label fine-tuning; no confidence loss, ensembling or loss variants.
Single 1.5B→2.8B pair; no weak-to-strong PGR across sizes or tasks.
The theory bounds KD versus standard training, not when a student must beat its supervisor.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's labels should be dropped. In particular, the V2 limits_scope claim (SALTDS below SALT on SuperGLUE) rests on misread columns: in fact SALTDS 65.58 > SALT 65.28. Many SALT/SALTDS domain rows took @70% values as @100%. Correct @100% values are SALT 22.70/54.55/61.67/48.30/65.28/4.73/17.00 and SALTDS 21.72/54.93/62.10/53.00/65.58/4.83/17.80. The study's ground-truth loss term means teacher-exceeding results cannot evidence weak-to-strong generalization.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses weak-model soft labels mixed with ground-truth next-token supervision during pre-training, not fine-tuning on weak labels alone. It does not calculate PGR or directly report a strong model trained on true labels as a ceiling in the PGR formula.

It compares early-stage KD, data selection, and transition strategies, but does not report PGR. It does not test auxiliary confidence losses, ensembling weak supervisors, or the loss variants named in the claim.

It reports results across NLP benchmark domains and compares a more-trained teacher in an appendix, but does not sweep student size, test chess or reward modelling, or study representations as predictors. PGR is not computed.
The paper does not test supervisor-checking failures, distribution shift, or whether shared errors between weak and strong models reduce gains.
The theory concerns KD generalization and bias-variance trade-offs; it does not establish conditions under which a student must beat its supervisor.

relation.reason: Section 6 contrasts its pre-training setting with prior alignment work citing Burns et al.; it neither tests nor relies on the catalogued weak-to-strong effect.

tranche.reason: The study evaluates small-model-assisted pre-training with ground-truth supervision throughout, rather than fine-tuning a pretrained strong model on weak labels. Its risk bounds compare KD with standard pre-training, without establishing that a student must outperform its supervisor.

source_check.notes: All eight rows match Tables 2 and 7. KD uses teacher-loss weight 0.667 alongside ground-truth-loss weight 0.333; SALT then switches to pure ground-truth training, so these results do not isolate weak-label generalization.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: SALT and SALTDS at final pre-training checkpoints; held-out Pile accuracy and most reported few-shot domain aggregates
reader_labels.reason: The larger students trained with early weak-teacher KD exceed the SLM teacher; SALT and SALTDS also exceed the standard-pretrained large model on the aggregate few-shot score (R7, R9, R14, R15, R19, R20, R29, R30, R34, R40, R44, R45, R50, R52).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Full-duration KD (RKD), and domains where SALT variants remain below the standard-pretraining reference
reader_labels.reason: RKD is above the teacher on average few-shot performance but below standard pre-training, and its held-out log perplexity is worse than the SLM's; several SALT domain averages are also below standard pre-training (R6, R13, R18, R23, R24, R25, R28, R33, R35, R38, R48).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Early KD with SALT, and SALT's tested transition range
reader_labels.reason: SALT and SALTDS exceed the standard-pretraining average at 70% of steps; the transition sweep reports strong results at 20K–60K, while full-duration KD performs substantially worse (R49, R51, R53, R54, R55, R56).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: SALTDS versus SALT across evaluation domains
reader_labels.reason: Data selection does not improve every domain: SALTDS is below SALT on SuperGLUE, while it is above SALT on other reported domain averages (R34, R35, R39, R40).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The size of the student advantage varies by domain: results range from modest gains over the teacher and/or standard baseline to larger gains, and some SALT variants fall below standard pre-training in particular domains (R13-R15, R18-R20, R23-R25, R28-R30, R33-R35, R38-R40, R43-R45).
